questions.q: What two conditions must a set of vectors {e_1, ..., e_n} satisfy to count as an orthonormal basis?
options: Each vector has norm 1 (<e_i|e_i> = 1), and every distinct pair has inner product 0 (<e_i|e_j> = 0 for i != j)
Each vector must have norm greater than 1, and all pairs must have equal inner products
All vectors must be identical to each other
Each vector must have at least one real entry and one complex entry
questions.explain: Orthonormal combines two separate requirements: 'ortho' (distinct vectors have zero inner product) and 'normal' (each vector has unit norm). Both must hold for every vector and every pair.

questions.q: For e_1 = (1/sqrt(2))(1,1) and e_2 = (1/sqrt(2))(1,-1), what does computing <e_1|e_2> confirm?
options: <e_1|e_2> = 0, confirming the two vectors are orthogonal, which together with their unit norms makes {e_1, e_2} an orthonormal basis
<e_1|e_2> = 1, meaning the vectors are identical
<e_1|e_2> is undefined because the vectors have fractional entries
<e_1|e_2> = 2, meaning the vectors point in the same direction
questions.explain: Working out (1/2)[1*1 + 1*(-1)] = (1/2)(0) = 0 confirms orthogonality. Combined with <e_1|e_1> = <e_2|e_2> = 1, this set qualifies as an orthonormal basis.

questions.q: How is the projection operator P_0 = |0><0| constructed, and what matrix does it give for |0> = (1,0)?
options: It is built as an outer product with entries a_i*(b_j)*, giving the matrix [[1,0],[0,0]] for |0> = (1,0)
It is built as an inner product, giving a single number rather than a matrix
It is the identity matrix [[1,0],[0,1]], regardless of which basis vector is used
It is built by adding |0> to its own conjugate transpose
questions.explain: The outer product |0><0| has entries (|0><0|)_ij = (0_i)(0_j)*, which for |0>=(1,0) works out entry by entry to [[1,0],[0,0]] -- a matrix, not a number, which is what distinguishes an outer product from an inner product.

questions.q: Applying P_0 = [[1,0],[0,0]] to |psi> = (0.6, 0.8i) gives the result (0.6, 0). How does this result relate to <0|psi>?
options: The result equals <0|psi> times |0>, where <0|psi> = 0.6 is the amplitude for the |0> component of |psi>
The result is unrelated to <0|psi>; it is simply the original vector unchanged
The result equals <0|psi> times |1>, swapping which basis vector is kept
The result is always the zero vector regardless of |psi>
questions.explain: P_0|psi> = <0|psi>|0> is the general pattern for any projection: here <0|psi> = 0.6, and multiplying by |0> = (1,0) gives exactly (0.6, 0), matching the direct matrix computation.

questions.q: Why does measurement in quantum computing rely specifically on projecting onto the directions of an ORTHONORMAL basis, rather than any arbitrary set of vectors?
options: Only with an orthonormal basis do the projections avoid double-counting any part of the state, so the resulting outcome probabilities correctly add up to 1
Orthonormal bases are required only because they are easier to write down on paper
Any set of vectors works identically well for measurement, orthonormal or not
Orthonormal bases guarantee that a qubit can only ever be measured as |0>
questions.explain: Projecting onto an orthonormal basis's directions cleanly decomposes a state with no overlap between components, which is exactly what is needed for the resulting measurement outcome probabilities to sum to 1.
